text: Settled comfortably, snugly, or securely into a place, often somewhere protective or hard to dislodge from. The kilogram cylinder is ensconced in three protective glass jars, and the article jokes that the Big Mac is likewise ensconced in its cardboard box.

Loud, harsh, and insistently forceful, in a way that is hard to ignore and often grates on listeners. Calling Trump the most strident critic of cheap Asian currencies means he complains about them the loudest and most aggressively of any world leader.

A state of loud confusion, disorder, or upheaval, whether in a crowd, a market, or a life. Currency tumult here means exchange rates swinging around while politicians argue about what they should be worth.

Bell-shaped glass domes placed over delicate objects to protect them from dust and air. The standard kilogram sits under three of them, nested like Russian dolls, because even a speck of dust would technically change the world's definition of a kilogram.

A metal made by blending two or more metals to get better properties than either alone, like steel or bronze. Le Grand K is a platinum alloy (platinum mixed with iridium) chosen because it barely corrodes or wears.

Made or shaped, originally by heating and hammering metal. Watch this word: it can also mean faked, as in a forged signature, but here both the platinum cylinder and the index were forged in the making sense, crafted in London.

French for The Great K, the nickname of the platinum cylinder near Paris that officially defined the kilogram from 1889 until 2019. Every scale on Earth ultimately traced its accuracy back to this one object.
Final, authoritative, and settling the matter; the version everything else is judged against. Le Grand K was the definitive standard for the kilogram, meaning by definition it could not be wrong.
Weight or substance, literally how heavy something feels when you lift it. Monetary heft is a playful way of saying how much weight a currency really carries, how much it can actually buy.

What a unit of money can actually buy in goods and services. A currency with high purchasing power stretches far at the store. The article argues this, not the number on a currency exchange screen, is a currency's true value.
Here this means an option being considered for a role, not a person running for office. The Big Mac is The Economist's favourite candidate for the job of measuring currencies.
The nickname for McDonald's giant yellow M logo, and by extension for McDonald's itself. Finding something under two Golden Arches just means finding it at a McDonald's.
The Economist's half-serious measure of currencies, started in 1986. It compares the price of a Big Mac across countries to judge whether each currency is priced above or below its real buying power.

An experiment you run purely in your head, imagining a scenario to test an idea when you cannot try it physically. Einstein imagined riding a beam of light; The Economist imagined using a burger to measure currencies.

t: take on a life of its own
forms: taken on a life of its own
text: To grow beyond what its creator planned and keep going on its own momentum. The index was meant as a one-off joke, but forty years later textbooks and academics treat it seriously.

The official institutions that manage a country's money, like America's Federal Reserve. They set interest rates and influence what a currency is worth, which is why an index calling their currency mispriced can irritate them.
Relating to money and currency. High monetary diplomacy means top-level negotiations between governments about money matters, in this case what their currencies should be worth against each other.
Worried, especially in a nagging, ongoing way. Policymakers fretted that currencies were badly mispriced, meaning the worry gnawed at them constantly rather than striking once.

Out of proper position relative to something else, like car wheels pointing in slightly different directions. Misaligned currencies are priced out of line with their true buying power, some too expensive and some too cheap.
A disaster; an event causing great damage. Financial calamity here means something like a market crash or currency crisis that mispriced currencies were feared to invite.

The policy of shielding your country's industries from foreign competition using tariffs, quotas, and other barriers to imports. It protects local jobs in the short run but tends to raise prices and invite retaliation from trading partners.
Literally means pleasant to taste, and more broadly means acceptable or agreeable. Calling the index a palatable guide is a double pun: it is easy to swallow both as food and as economics.
Unconventional and slightly odd, departing from what is expected. Using fast food to measure world currencies seems an eccentric choice, which is exactly why the article then defends it.

To adjust something precisely against a standard so it performs exactly the same every time. McDonald's calibrates the Big Mac's taste and texture worldwide the way scientists calibrate instruments, which is what makes it usable as a measuring stick.
Careful, persistent effort and attention to detail. The joke is that McDonald's guards the sameness of its burger with the same diligence scientists devoted to the sacred kilogram cylinder.
To pour something out generously, almost extravagantly, on someone or something. Scientists lavished care on the kilogram cylinder, meaning they gave it enormous, even excessive, attention.

forms: bang you can get for your buck
text: Value received for money spent; how much you really get for each dollar. A common American idiom: more bang for your buck means a better deal.
The global marketplace where currencies are traded for one another and where exchange rates are set, minute by minute. Often shortened to forex, it is the biggest financial market in the world.
Wandered away from where something belongs. Saying currencies have strayed far from their purchasing power means their market prices have drifted well away from their fair values.

Telling you how things ought to be, rather than describing how they are. The article sorts doubts about the index into three kinds: predictive (will it forecast rates?), descriptive (does it capture reality?), and prescriptive (should it guide what rates ought to be?).
Informal for power, energy, or punch. Judging the oomph of currencies means judging how much real buying strength each one has.

Here an adjective meaning detailed and complex, with many carefully worked-out parts. The World Bank's elaborate price comparisons cover thousands of products in dozens of countries, the opposite of the one-burger shortcut.

A delay between something happening and its effects or measurements appearing. The World Bank's price data arrives with a long lag: numbers about 2021 were not published until 2024, by which time the world had moved on.

Literally to break down food, but also to absorb and make sense of information. Saying the index is easier to digest is another food pun: it is simpler to understand than the World Bank's giant datasets.
Judged or officially considered to be something. Only seven economies were deemed cheap by one measure but expensive by the other, meaning the two measures mostly agree in their verdicts.

A common food additive used to thicken sauces and keep ingredients from separating. It is named here to show the Big Mac is secretly a bundle of over 60 ingredients, which is part of why it reflects a whole economy.
Priced higher than something is really worth. An overvalued currency costs more on the exchange markets than its actual buying power justifies, making that country feel expensive to visitors.

Priced lower than something is really worth. An undervalued currency is cheaper to buy than its purchasing power justifies, which makes that country's goods a bargain for foreigners and gives its exporters an edge.
Out of balance or proper working order. A machine, a schedule, or here a set of currencies can be out of kilter, meaning things are misadjusted relative to how they should be.

The International Monetary Fund, an organisation of about 190 countries that watches over the world economy, lends to governments in trouble, and publishes influential estimates like the one saying China's currency is 16% too weak.

The basic underlying facts about an economy, like its growth, productivity, trade, and inflation, as opposed to market moods and speculation. Saying the yuan is weaker than fundamentals imply means its low price cannot be explained by the real economy.
An advantage that lets you beat rivals. A cheap currency gives a country's exporters a competitive edge because their goods look like bargains to foreign buyers.
To accumulate or pile up, usually quickly, like racking up points in a game or charges on a credit card. China has racked up enormous trade surpluses, meaning they have piled up year after year.

When a country sells more to the rest of the world than it buys from it. China's trade surplus in goods neared $1.2 trillion last year, and its trading partners complain a too-cheap yuan is part of the reason.

Deadly; capable of causing death or destruction. A mortal threat to European industry is one that could kill it off entirely, not merely wound it. The word comes from the Latin for death, as in mortality.
To give in, soften, or back down from a hard position. Macron's threat only matters if China does not relent, that is, if it refuses to change course on its currency.

To deliberately lower the value of your own currency against others. It sounds self-defeating, but a cheaper currency makes your exports cheaper abroad, which is why Trump accused China and Japan of always wanting to devalue.
To fade, recede, or grow weaker, the way the tide ebbs away from the shore. Talk of currency fights from the White House has ebbed, meaning it has quieted down lately.
Filled with excited talk and activity, like a beehive humming. Currency traders are abuzz with rumours, meaning the gossip has everyone chattering.

A famous 1985 deal, signed at New York's Plaza Hotel, in which America, Japan, Britain, France, and West Germany agreed to act together to push down an over-strong dollar. Traders still invoke its name whenever they suspect governments might team up on exchange rates again.
A formal agreement or deal between parties, often countries. The Plaza Accord was a pact among five governments to steer the dollar's value down together.

An exchange rate after adjusting for prices in each country, measuring what your money actually buys rather than the raw conversion number. In economics the word real is a trap: it means adjusted for prices or inflation, not genuine as opposed to fake.

How much a country's own people spend on goods and services at home. Low domestic consumption in China means Chinese households spend relatively little of what the country produces, so the extra output gets exported instead.
Wide open and gaping, like a mouth mid-yawn. A yawning budget deficit is a huge one. The word has nothing to do with being sleepy here; it is a vivid way of saying the gap is enormous.
The gap when a government spends more in a year than it collects in taxes, covered by borrowing. America's yawning budget deficit is part of the imbalance the article links to mispriced currencies.

Tending to push prices down across an economy. Falling prices sound nice but are dangerous: shoppers delay purchases waiting for cheaper deals, businesses earn less, and the whole economy can stall. China's deflationary tendencies are a sign of weak demand.
The official residence of the president of France, in Paris, France's equivalent of the White House. The article mentions it to place Le Grand K's vault about 10km away.

No longer needed because something else already does the job. If exchange rates ever matched purchasing power perfectly, the Big Mac index would have nothing left to reveal and would become redundant.
Drifting free, like a boat cut loose from its mooring at the dock. Currencies that remain unmoored have no anchor tying their market prices to their true buying power.
Unpleasant or offensive, literally something that tastes bad. The article's final pun: critics find the burger index distasteful, but it plans to keep serving it anyway.
